title: Annual Economic Report 2026, Chapter I: Progress and peril
key_claim: The BIS warns that the global economy has become unusually reliant on a single AI-related investment boom; the five largest hyperscalers are set to spend more than USD 1 trillion on AI capex over 2025-2026, with commitments outpacing earnings and free cash flow and pushing firms toward debt and opaque circular financing. The report draws parallels with canal mania and the dot-com crash and warns that a disappointment in returns could trigger a sudden withdrawal of financing, turning a capex boom into a protracted investment bust with knock-on effects across the financial system.
frame_summary: The BIS argues the AI investment boom has become a systemic financial-stability risk because its sustainability hinges on hyperscaler earnings meeting very high expectations amid rising debt and concentration.
notes: Tier-1 macro anchor for 'why it matters at scale': the earnings-expectation dependence and the capex-outrunning-cash-flow / debt-financing point. Chapter I of the flagship Annual Economic Report, published 28 June 2026 (meta DC.date 2026-06-28; press release p260628). Not used for the depreciation-accounting mechanism itself.

title: Global Financial Stability Report, April 2026 (Chapter 1)
key_claim: The IMF identifies stretched valuations and concentration in AI-related firms as a material downside risk to financial stability, and its April 2026 GFSR states that elevated leverage financing AI-related investment, coupled with rapid capital-obsolescence risks, increases uncertainty around future earnings and asset valuations.
frame_summary: The IMF argues that AI-related market concentration, leverage and rapid capital obsolescence together heighten the risk of an abrupt correction in earnings and valuations.
notes: Second Tier-1 anchor and the one that most directly links the signal's mechanism: 'rapid capital-obsolescence risks' feeding 'uncertainty around future earnings and asset valuations' (GFSR Ch.1). Landing page (14/04/2026) confirms date via meta-Date and meta-parsely-pub-date. Chapter 1 full PDF at .../april/english/ch1.pdf. In-window at 88 days.

title: Tracking Trillions: The Assumptions Shaping the Scale of the AI Build-Out
date_evidence: George Lee ... May 1, 2026 (dateline directly under the article title)
key_claim: The economic useful life of AI silicon is the single most influential variable in determining the scale of cumulative AI infrastructure investment. AI accelerators have a useful life typically estimated at four to six years, but NVIDIA's roughly annual release cadence and step-change generational gains mean many analysts believe the prevailing four-to-six-year depreciation treatment is less reflective of the assets' real value; extending or shortening assumed life moves cumulative spend and annual depreciation by hundreds of billions of dollars, and accounting statements may show orderly depreciation while operational obsolescence imposes a very different economic reality that can arrive abruptly.
frame_summary: Goldman Sachs argues that GPU useful-life assumptions are the biggest supply-side swing variable in the AI build-out, and that prevailing depreciation schedules may understate how fast frontier silicon becomes uneconomic.
notes: Key Tier-2 anchor for the depreciation mechanism. Goldman Sachs Global Institute (not GS Global Investment Research). Dateline 'May 1, 2026' on the page. Baseline ~USD 7.6tn cumulative AI capex 2026-2031; buildings depreciated ~20yr and power ~25yr vs silicon on far shorter cycles; H100/A100 rental prices cited both ways.

title: The AI boom has doubled computing infrastructure's share of US GDP
date_evidence: Data Insight, Jun. 5, 2026 (byline, Isabel Juniewicz); meta-pagefind:date: Fri Jun 05 2026
key_claim: Investment in AI-related data-center construction, compute hardware and networking accounted for about 0.8% of US GDP in Q1 2026, driving computing infrastructure as a whole to about 1.5% of GDP, up from a 2015-2022 average of about 0.7%; AI infrastructure is now the leading driver of growth in US private investment.
frame_summary: Epoch AI argues the AI buildout has more than doubled computing infrastructure's share of US GDP since 2023 and is now the leading driver of private-investment growth.
notes: Tier-2 macro-scale anchor quantifying the economy's exposure to the buildout. Uses BEA/Census/FRED series. Data insight dated 5 June 2026 (byline and meta-pagefind date).

title: Meta: Accounting for AI Data Center Depreciation (HBS Case 126-034)
date_evidence: Publications: June 2026 ... Citation: 'Harvard Business School Case 126-034, June 2026.'
key_claim: In early 2026 Meta's capital expenditure was climbing from USD 72.2 billion in 2025 to a projected USD 135 billion in 2026, largely for data centers and GPUs. Alongside the buildout Meta extended the useful life of its servers and network assets from four years to five and a half, a revision that reduced 2025 depreciation expense by USD 2.9 billion; every major hyperscaler made similar extensions between 2020 and 2025. Short sellers argued the changes overstated profits by understating the true pace of GPU obsolescence, while management pointed to improved hardware reliability, software efficiency and operational experience.
frame_summary: The HBS case argues that depreciation assumptions have become a central lever on hyperscaler reported earnings, framing Meta's useful-life extension as an accounting judgement with large profit consequences.
notes: Tier-2 anchor for the Meta useful-life extension (4 to 5.5 years; USD 2.9bn 2025 depreciation reduction) and the short-seller overstatement argument. HBS Case Collection, June 2026 (Heese, Korganbekova, Pinckney). Landing page is free; full case is paywalled, but the abstract carries the load-bearing figures. Page build date (2026-07-11) is not the publication date; publication is 'June 2026'.

title: The AI boom's historical warning
key_claim: Reporting on the BIS Annual Economic Report, Axios notes the global economy is unusually reliant on a single AI investment boom, and that if investors question AI's payoff, hyperscalers could pull back on spending, leaving suppliers that expanded and took on debt struggling to service it, with stress able to spread through the fast-growing private-credit market and a US-led equity repricing propagating globally.
frame_summary: Axios argues the AI buildout rhymes with historic investment booms that ended in busts, and that the economy's dependence on it makes an earnings disappointment a systemic risk.
notes: Tier-3 quality-journalism corroboration of the BIS macro-dependence framing, dated 30 June 2026 (meta article:published_time). Used to anchor the 'earnings disappointment is a macro/financing event' link in the body.

title: Hyperscaler Depreciation Schedules and AI Capex Circularity: The $200 Billion Earnings Question
key_claim: Microsoft, Google, Meta and Oracle each extended assumed server/networking useful life from roughly four years to five or six between 2022 and 2024, with disclosed first-year benefits totalling more than USD 10 billion; in February 2025 Amazon broke ranks, shortening a subset of servers from six years back to five, citing the 'increased pace of technology development, particularly in the area of artificial intelligence and machine learning', and taking a USD 920 million accelerated-depreciation charge. A four-year counterfactual against the affected base and projected 2026-2028 capex implies roughly USD 228 billion of suppressed depreciation (rounded to about USD 200 billion), close to Michael Burry's published USD 176 billion estimate for 2026-2028.
frame_summary: Footnote Brief argues that hyperscaler useful-life extensions have inflated reported AI-era earnings by roughly USD 200 billion through 2028, with Amazon's reversal the cleanest signal the longer schedules are aggressive.
notes: Tier-4 independent analyst blog, used only as directional corroboration for the concrete divergence (Amazon 6->5, USD 920m charge, Feb 2025) and the USD 176-230bn earnings-suppression range. Amazon quote is from Amazon's own 10-K per the piece. Published 21 May 2026 (meta article:published_time). The signal rests on the Tier-1/2 sources; this source adds specificity, not the anchor.
